procedure.step: Register the factory with the Ministry of Economy and Tourism through the Factory Registration service, which requires the factory to be located outside a free zone, a MoIAT industrial licence, and a MoIAT letter confirming 40% domestic value added; processing takes about 3 working days.
procedure.authority: the Ministry of Economy and Tourism

procedure.step: Prepare the documents needed for the certificate application: proof of factory registration, the commercial invoice, and, if a trading exporter, the factory's purchase invoice.
Log in to the ministry e-services portal and choose the Certificate of Origin for India service.
Fill in the application form with the HS code, description, quantity and value of the exported product; each item must qualify separately.
Pay the certificate fee: AED 50 (band: invoice value up to AED 100000).
Receive the approval, or a return with comments to correct; then print the approved certificate. Processing takes about one working day.
Ensure the certificate is issued prior to, at, or within 5 working days of the date of exportation. It is valid for 12 months from issue and covers only one import.
If needed, a certificate can be issued retrospectively up to 12 months from the date of shipment, marked 'ISSUED RETROSPECTIVELY' in box 9 (Remarks) of India's certificate form.

Ship the goods directly from the UAE to India. Transit through another country is allowed only under customs control, with no operations other than unloading, reloading, storage or similar. If a third party issues the invoice, the exporter must indicate 'third-party invoicing'.

Give the certificate to the Indian importer, who will claim the CEPA rate when filing the bill of entry. The importer must hold origin information and keep supporting documents for at least 5 years from filing, and answer a customs request within 10 working days.
Keep origin records, including the cost breakdown, for at least 5 years starting from the end of the year of the certificate's issue.

caveats.note: The '+' in the rule is read as 'and' (both tests must pass). The agreement does not define '+', so this is Mansha's interpretation.
Operations and final manufacture are the exporter's own declaration.
Factory declared in a free zone: likely not eligible for the ministry's factory registration; confirm with the ministry.
The duty estimate is on the shipment value given. India charges duty on the assessable (CIF) value at import, so actual amounts will differ.
The CEPA rate reduces Basic Customs Duty (BCD) only. IGST, GST compensation cess, Social Welfare Surcharge and any anti-dumping or safeguard duty still apply.
The CEPA rate applies only if the product qualifies under the rules of origin and a valid certificate of origin is presented.
'Direct labour cost' and 'direct overhead cost' are not defined in the agreement.
The agreement does not say whether the build-down and build-up methods use the same threshold, apart from the 5-point Ex-Works adjustment.
Interpretation: de minimis helps only the tariff-shift part of a rule, not the VA percentage.
The certificate form discrepancy: the agreement says box 8, but India's origin rules and certificate form say box 9; India's form governs entry into India.
UAE law sets a shorter 3-year minimum for record keeping; the CEPA's 5 years governs CEPA claims.

No official page read names the Ministry of Foreign Trade as the issuer of the India CEPA certificate specifically: its service page covers preferential certificates in general, and the India-specific page is still on moet.gov.ae.
Fee bands are in AED and apply to the invoice value in AED; no currency conversion is done by Mansha.
Electronic certificates are reportedly accepted and uploaded to India's e-Sanchit system, but this is from secondary sources, not confirmed.
